title: Bhagavato
hook: two translation apps, two English lines, one Pali title
tomorrow: what makes someone worthy of joined palms?

segments.voice: Yesterday, namo: homage, a bow in a word, and tassa, a pointer where a name would go. Homage to him. Today, the first of the three titles that tell you who.

Paste one sentence into two translation apps and you often get two English lines, both a little right. The third word of the homage has had that happen for a long time. Bhagavato. On a Theravada chant sheet it usually reads: to the Blessed One. Rhys Davids, translating the suttas into English, wrote the Blessed One. Other translators chose the Lord, or the Exalted One. And underneath all of them sits an older argument, inside the tradition itself, about what the title even points to.
screen: `TWO APPS, TWO LINES.` → `BLESSED ONE? LORD? EXALTED ONE?` → `AN OLDER ARGUMENT.`

segments.voice: First the grammar, because it's quick. The title is bhagava. The ending on bhagavato does what tassa's ending did: it carries the to. To the Blessed One. Now the argument. Buddhaghosa's Path of Purification, the great Theravada handbook, explains the title several ways and keeps them all. Two of them pull in different directions. The first view hears bhaga, fortune, a share of good. The Blessed One is the fortunate one: the one whose long training ripened into something rich enough to give away. Its best case: it tells you why people bow. He has something to share, and the homage is thanks. The second view hears bhagga, broken. The Blessed One is the one who broke greed, hatred and delusion. Its best case: it puts the weight on what he did, and a breaking is something others can train toward too. Fortune names what he holds; broken names what he let go. The handbook doesn't crown either one. It lists them side by side, and the chant carries both in a single word. So when you say bhagavato, you can hear the bow of thanks, or the sound of something snapping, or both. That's the Blessed One: a title wide enough for an argument.
screen: `THE ENDING CARRIES THE TO.` · `VIEW ONE: BHAGA, FORTUNE.` · `VIEW TWO: BHAGGA, BROKEN.` · `THE HANDBOOK KEEPS BOTH.` · then, large: `THE BLESSED ONE.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on one thing you honor: a photo of someone who taught you, a Buddha image if you keep one, a plant someone gave you. Softly say namo tassa bhagavato, feeling the breath in the bh, then keep looking at it until the words have settled.
Bhagavato. To the Blessed One: the fortunate one, or the one who broke greed, hatred and delusion. The handbook keeps both readings. Word five of a little Pali.
Your line: the Blessed One, a title wide enough for an argument. Five words into the block.

chat.says: poster says 'the Blessed One.' Ava asked, blessed by who? i had nothing.
options: Nobody bestowed it. One reading: his training ripened into fortune. Another: he broke greed.
By God. In Pali, bhagavato means the one God chose and blessed with awakening.
By his followers. It is an honor title the monks gave him only after he died.
chat.meaning: Buddhaghosa reads bhagava as the fortunate one, or the one who broke greed, hatred and delusion, and keeps both. Neither is a blessing given from outside.
